# []{#anchor}Notation

This chapter lists the mathematical symbols, abbreviations and statistics used in the report, with the units of each and where it is defined. The complete set, including quantities that appear only in the Methods Supplement, is given in the Methods Supplement, Appendix C.

## []{#anchor}Statistics, and how to read them

  ----------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **NSE** (Nash--Sutcliffe Efficiency)                  How much of the observed variance the simulated series reproduces, relative to simply predicting the record mean                                                           −∞ to 1                                                                A value of 1 is a perfect forecast; a value of 0 indicates the model does no better than the mean; negative values indicate it does worse                                                   Iterative NSE is the study's hardest test, because the model is run forward from one initial condition and its errors compound. The SSM-over-TLM gain, ΔNSE, is what quantifies the value of the explicit drainage term, and it is one of the three axes on which the five clusters separate
  **RMSE** (root mean square error)                     Typical size of the model's error, in the units of the thing being modelled                                                                                                ≥ 0                                                                    Lower is better; the meaningful comparison is against the observed range, not against zero                                                                                                  Reported in metres of head. It is the metric that makes the EWI's calibration onto the MSL5 scale legible, because it says how far a predicted level typically sits from the measured one
  **Bias**                                              Mean signed error: whether the model sits systematically high or low, as opposed to merely scattered                                                                       any sign                                                               A value near zero is good; a bias comparable to the RMSE indicates a systematic offset rather than noise                                                                                    Bias is the statistic that separates the EWI's known systematic depth offset from random error. A model can have acceptable RMSE and still be unusable as a level if the bias is large
  **R²** (coefficient of determination)                 Fraction of variance in the response explained by the fitted model                                                                                                         0 to 1 for a fitted OLS model                                          Higher is better, but a high value on a one-step fit is a weak claim                                                                                                                        Applied to the one-step SSM fit, R² is generous, because last month's level does most of the work. Prefer iterative NSE for any claim about predictive skill
  **Pearson r**                                         Strength of the straight-line relationship between two variables                                                                                                           −1 to +1                                                               Values near ±1 indicate a tight linear relationship; values near 0 indicate none                                                                                                            Pearson r is the affinity measure that classifies extended-network wells against cluster centroids, and the threshold for Multi-Cluster Affinity is set on it. It is sensitive to shape, not to amplitude, which is why a well can be affine to several centroids at once
  **Spearman ρ**                                        Strength of the monotone relationship between the *ranks* of two variables                                                                                                 −1 to +1                                                               Values near ±1 indicate a consistent ordering; values near 0 indicate none                                                                                                                  Used where the ordering matters and the functional form does not --- the coastal-end ordering of anchor-referenced levels, and peak rainfall lag against ridge distance. Being rank-based, it is not distorted by one extreme well
  **VIF** (variance inflation factor)                   How much wider a coefficient's error bar is because that predictor overlaps with the other predictors                                                                      ≥ 1                                                                    A value of 1 indicates no overlap. Values above about 5 warrant attention and above about 10 are conventionally treated as serious overlap; both are rules of thumb, not pipeline outputs   Consider what happens if rainfall, PET and antecedent displacement all rise and fall together: the fit cannot tell which of them is doing the work, so it spreads the credit arbitrarily and every coefficient's error bar widens. The VIF is exactly how much wider --- a VIF of 4 indicates the variance is four times what it would be with independent predictors, so the error bar is twice as wide. In this study, it answers one specific worry: that C4 Main Forest's small β₃ is an artefact of PET and displacement moving together at a deep-water-table cluster rather than a real property of the cluster. The per-cluster values sit in `30_c4_identifiability_by_cluster.csv`, column `VIF`
  **Condition number**                                  How well-shaped the predictor data are as a whole, rather than one predictor at a time                                                                                     ≥ 1                                                                    A value near 1 indicates a well-shaped design. Large values indicate an ill-conditioned one; the conventional flag is above about 30, which is a rule of thumb, not a pipeline output       Picture every month of data as a point in a space with one axis per predictor. If those points form a roughly round cloud, the fit has seen every combination and stands on firm ground. If they form a long thin cigar, there is one direction the data barely explores, and the coefficients along it swing about wildly for tiny changes in the input. The condition number is how elongated that cigar is --- the longest axis divided by the shortest. Where VIF interrogates one predictor, the condition number interrogates the design as a whole, which is why the two are reported side by side; the value sits in `30_c4_identifiability_by_cluster.csv`, column `cond`
  **t-statistic**                                       Coefficient divided by its own standard error: how many error bars the estimate sits away from zero                                                                        any sign                                                               Magnitudes above about 2 correspond to significance at the conventional level for a reasonable sample; magnitudes below 1 indicate an estimate the data cannot separate from zero           Reported alongside every SSM and BACI coefficient. Because it is a ratio, a large t can come from a large effect or from a small standard error, so read it beside the coefficient itself and never on its own
  **p-value**                                           Probability of seeing an effect at least this large if the true effect were zero                                                                                           0 to 1                                                                 Values below `DETECTABILITY_ALPHA` = 0.05 are treated as significant; values just either side of it are treated as inconclusive rather than as decisive                                     The study's convention is that a non-significant result indicates the record cannot resolve the effect, not that the effect is absent. Language is kept to "consistent with" and "indicates" for that reason
  **AIC and ΔAIC**                                      Model fit penalized for the number of parameters, so that a more complex model has to earn its extra terms                                                                 AIC on an arbitrary scale; ΔAIC is the difference between two models   Only differences mean anything. A ΔAIC below −2 indicates the more complex model is worth keeping; a value near zero indicates the two forms are indistinguishable                          AIC is what decides whether the depth-dependent PET term is retained over fixed β₂, and whether the curvature terms are retained in the BACI specification. Where the linear-capped and exponential coastal decay forms sit within a couple of AIC units of each other, the choice between them is a methods footnote rather than a headline decision
  **Confidence interval**                               Range of values the data are consistent with, at a stated level of confidence                                                                                              as the quantity                                                        An interval excluding zero indicates a resolved effect; a wide interval indicates a poorly constrained one even where the point estimate looks large                                        The study prefers the interval to the point estimate throughout. Two intervals that overlap do not by themselves indicate two quantities are equal, which is why the seasonal gradient question is settled by a single interaction test rather than by comparing two subset fits
  **Bootstrap CI**                                      Confidence interval built by resampling the data many times and reading the spread of the answers, rather than by assuming a distribution                                  as the quantity                                                        Read exactly as any other interval; a bootstrap interval much wider than the analytic one indicates the analytic assumptions were optimistic                                                Used where the analytic form is not trustworthy: a moving-block resample preserves the seasonal structure of a monthly series, and a well-level resample answers the different question of how much the answer depends on which wells are in the cluster. The block length, replicate count and seed are fixed in `config.py`, so an interval reproduces exactly
  **AR(1) correction and effective N**                  Adjustment for the fact that consecutive observations in a time series carry overlapping information, so the record holds fewer independent data points than it has rows   effective N ≤ N                                                        An effective N far below N indicates that an uncorrected p-value would be badly overconfident                                                                                               Trend significance is quoted on the AR(1)-corrected footing throughout --- `p_ar` in `32_site_mean_trend.csv`, not `p_ols` --- because an annual spring series of two decades can carry an effective sample size of only about five. This is the single correction that most changes which trends the study is willing to call resolved
  **Statistical power and minimum detectable effect**   The size of effect the record could have detected, had one been present                                                                                                    as the quantity                                                        A minimum detectable effect larger than the effect of interest indicates the analysis cannot settle the question either way                                                                 Reported alongside every site-mean trend as `min_detectable_mm_yr` in `32_site_mean_trend.csv`, computed at `DETECTABILITY_ALPHA` = 0.05 and `DIFF_POWER_TARGET` = 0.80. It is what turns a null result into a statement about the record rather than about the site: where the minimum detectable rate exceeds the rate being looked for, the correct reading is that the record is too short, not that nothing is happening
